tiers.name: Open
tiers.meaning: Internal or personal route: campus bodies, alumni cell, professional bodies with a direct, disclosed introduction

tiers.name: Cold but reachable

central: The central idea. The Neural Network should not sell itself as a college club looking for logos. It should offer partners a well-scoped way to meet curious management students, test a business use case, teach a practical skill or build a responsible student community. The strongest first move is a small pilot with a clear owner and output. Earn the right to ask for recurring support only after the pilot works.

The positioning. The club's edge is a management lens: students who work out how an AI tool makes money, fits into an enterprise workflow or scales across tier-2 markets. Pitch the cohort's management perspective. Do not promise campus footfall, internships, attendee data or exclusivity.

items.t: Maintain one verified, tiered list of every partner, speaker and collaborator proposed, each matched to a specific ask and a template.
Internal (committee and Outreach team); the list directs all external contact.

The outreach plan names about forty external targets and the curation plan names more (campus clubs, committees, guests). Without a single list, the same organisation (Futurense, Sarvam AI and Unstop each appear in several target lists) would be approached several times by different people.

Test each name against four questions: Is there a visible reason to engage? Is there a published channel? Does the club have something specific to offer? Is the ask small? Order by speed of reply, not by prestige. Skip global giants whose outreach dies in a PR inbox.

Internal only. Each row records access tier, purpose, ask, contact route and its source page, confidence, fallback, template and two separate ratings: priority (how much the partner matters) and chance of a first yes.

Mark conflicts of interest and personal connections for disclosure.

A single source of truth and a sequenced attack order.
Notes on every touch are kept in the pipeline ledger (V2-02).
Share of rows with a verified contact route and source page; duplicates avoided; targets contacted against plan.

initiatives.title: Outreach Operating System: pipeline, approvals and contact hygiene

items.t: Run every external contact through one disciplined process so that it is fast, honest and tracked.
Internal; indirectly every partner.
Good execution beats a long list: an owner, a rhythm and a next action for every conversation. A visible ledger supports this.
Not applicable (internal process); target selection is in V2-01.

First email under 150 words, one specific ask, personalised with one verified detail; one follow-up after four to seven working days, then stop; one person per organisation and no bulk copies; do not attach the year plan, send a one-page note on a single event; LinkedIn contextual request only where a public profile exists, not repeated messages across channels.

Six stages: (1) Prepare: a one-page concept note, approved date range, event owner, expected participants, delivery format, estimated budget, what the partner is asked to provide. (2) Prioritise: days 1 to 2, start with the clearest routes. (3) Contact: days 2 to 4, official route first. (4) Follow up: once, after four to five business days. (5) Confirm: speaker, date, format, consent to record, promotional approvals, API or demo access, budget, travel and cancellation terms, in writing. (6) Close the loop: within five days send thanks, attendance and feedback summary, approved photos or links, outcomes and one specific next-step proposal.

Approvals: the faculty advisor approves the target, event and wording and is copied on every mail; nothing goes out on institute letterhead without approval; any company approach for a festival goes through the Industrial Relations and Sponsorship Committee first.

Contact hygiene: no guessed emails, no wrong desk (sales, technical support or hiring addresses are not partnership contacts), no unearned promises (no guaranteed sign-ups, attendance, internships, funding or product adoption), refresh role and programme status before sending, disclose personal introductions and connections in the first line.
Pipeline ledger: a tracker of total, sent, in talks and locked, with status and next-step notes for every target.
First 30 days: week 1 build the pack; week 2 create momentum; weeks 3 to 4 convert one pilot.
Pipeline sheet, one-page event notes, approval email template, shared inbox or team address.
Outreach Lead (owner); Pipeline Keeper; Faculty Advisor.
Fewer wasted messages, no avoidable embarrassments, every conversation with a next action.
The ledger holds the history so that a change of committee does not break relationships.
Pipeline counts (targets contacted, replies, meetings, pilots agreed); share of messages approved before sending (target 100%); close-the-loop completed within five days (target 100%).
Give the team a ready, honest pitch for each purpose, built around what the partner gains.
Internal; indirectly all partners.

A request for money and a request for time are different letters. Nine purpose-built drafts, further templates and four categories with a selector are consolidated here, which avoids a new letter for every email.
Select the template by purpose, then fill from the partner's own recent, checked activity (a talk, event or page).

Message anatomy (consolidated): (1) one checked, specific first line about them; (2) who we are in one line; (3) one specific ask only; (4) what the partner gains, framed as a possible outcome not a promise; (5) what we handle: link, room, questions in advance, moderation, recap; (6) a small first step: fifteen-minute call, one mentor, or a ten-minute recorded answer to three questions; (7) cc the faculty advisor. Keep under about 150 words.

Templates (see Section 3.5): sponsor in cash or kind; expert session; co-host or platform; media partner; alumni mentor; community programme application and campus event sponsorship, workshop, peer-club collaboration, executive routing; returning mentor case clinic; sponsorship tiers with an offer of demo slots and honest product feedback; speaker, mentor, sponsor and collaborator templates.
Store templates in one place with a "before sending" caution for each.
Fill every bracket; never send with an invented number in a first email.

Offer only what the club controls. Replace any claim that cannot be backed by evidence, for example a stated audience size or a promise to bring a fixed number of teams, until the club has a record to cite.
Write one finished piece before approaching media.
Log each version used.
Template files; one-page concept note template; Field Guide excerpts and recap samples as proof of work.
Partnerships Manager; Social and Content Lead for supporting material; Faculty Advisor for approval.
Consistent, credible pitches and a higher reply rate.
Each reply and each decline is recorded and its reason noted for the next approach.
Reply rate by template; share of messages passing the "before sending" check; time from draft to approval.

initiatives.title: Neural Exchange: Expert and Industry Speaker Series

items.t: Bring one practitioner, academic or alumnus to the club roughly every month, in a format that is hands-on and not a product pitch.

AI startup founders, engineers and researchers, product managers, consultants, content creators, ethics professionals, finance and marketing professionals; IIT, IIM and IISc academics; named expert prospects.
Speakers are a common proposal, but a calendar dependent on outsiders stops when they do, so speakers are a bonus layered on a core that can run without them.

Match speakers to a narrow topic that the speaker actually works on and that fits a session (name the topic yourself; never ask a busy person to think of one). Use the partner portfolio (Section 3.6) and ask alumni and faculty for introductions.

Expert session template: a 30-minute online talk with ten minutes for questions, questions sent in advance, club handles link, room and recap; fallback of a ten-minute recorded reply to three student questions. For founders, a zero-prep fireside: no slide deck, a 45-minute moderated Q and A based on their recent posts. For an executive: 20 minutes of moderated discussion, 15 of demonstration, 10 of student questions.
Month 1 to 2: shortlist ten speakers.
From Month 2: one-page pitch to each, personalised.
Two weeks before: one-page guest brief: audience is mixed beginners, no product pitches, one hands-on moment, 20-minute talk plus 15 of questions, slides shared three days before.
One week before: collect eight student questions; test audio and video; assign a host and timekeeper.
Within three days after: send thanks, photos and feedback; ask about mentors, internships or a repeat session; log what the partner offered.
Fallback: alumni, seniors, faculty or local practitioners fill the slot in the same format.
Video platform, moderator, question form, recording consent, one-page brief.
Speaker Liaison (Outreach); Session Host; Curation Lead for topic fit.
A guest in about eight to ten months of the year; live demonstrations; referrals to further speakers.
Thank-you within three days, a feedback summary, an invitation to the next Demo Day, and one specific next step.
Guest sessions held; average rating; referrals gained; share of guest slots filled by the original target versus fallback.

initiatives.title: Industry Challenge and Live Projects Programme

items.t: Source real problem statements, mentors and judges from companies so that projects and case events have genuine stakes.
Startups and operators with product-adoption needs; analytics and automation firms; edtech partners; platforms that run case competitions.

Live projects with mentorship, a project ladder with industry judges, companies with a record of B-school case contests and enterprise problem statements, and a clinic or case-challenge model all fit here.

Look for companies that run B-school contests or need management-student feedback (Mu Sigma's Mureka contest; Futurense AI Clinic and Leadership Council; automation vendors with academic MoUs; workflow platforms that value product adoption; finance and platform firms).

Lead with a defined, small project: a one-session clinic, a case challenge, a three-week student pod. Value exchange: students stress-test a product or audit a funnel and send structured findings. Keep the scope small (one workshop, one challenge) before any recurring ask.
Choose two partner problem statements per term.
Convert each into a case pack (V1-09) or a Rung 3 project brief (V1-08).
Agree a deliverable format and publication permission in writing.
Provide a mentor from the partner for the Build Day or Demo Day if possible.
Return a short findings report within five days of delivery.
One-page project brief, partner contact, student pods, mentors, report template.
Industry Partnerships Lead; Projects Lead; Case Lead.
Real problems, feedback for partners and strong portfolio pieces.
Report back what students found, invite the partner to judge, and ask whether a second round is useful.
Partner problem statements adopted; projects with a partner mentor; partner satisfaction; repeat requests.
Use the institute's alumni as the warmest and cheapest source of speakers, mentors and judges.
IIM Sirmaur alumni working in AI, analytics, finance and technology roles; the Alumni Relations Cell.
The alumni cell ranks first on access; alumni serve on career panels, as a fallback for any cancelled guest and as Build Day mentors; template T5 is built for this.
Ask the Alumni Relations Cell, through the faculty advisor, for a list of alumni in AI and analytics roles; then search professional networks and ask the cell to vet.

Introduction first through the cell, then the alumnus letter: twenty minutes, how AI comes into your working day, what you would learn first in our place, one mistake to avoid; online on a weekday evening or a Friday.
Month 0: approach the cell through the faculty advisor.
Build a list of ten alumni; send the T5 letter after the introduction.
Schedule Friday talks and one careers panel.
Invite alumni as Build Day mentors and Demo Day judges.
Faculty advisor's introduction; alumni database access via the cell; video link.
Alumni Liaison (owner); Faculty Advisor.
Warm, reliable guests and mentors; a network that returns each year.
Annual "year in review" note to alumni; invitations to Demo Day; a thank-you after each contribution.
Alumni contacted and replying; sessions or mentorships delivered; alumni returning.
Run selected sessions with the clubs and committees that already do parts of this work better than a new club could.

Quizzar (quizzing), Datonics (IT and analytics), Finserve (finance), Markaizen (marketing), the Media Cell, the Training and Development Cell, the Entrepreneurship and Incubation Cell, the Industrial Relations and Sponsorship Committee; The Dialectical Society and the Media and Communications Committee.

A first year with a good idea gets further by asking existing bodies than by starting a rival, and none of the seven proposed sessions depends on a partner (if a body declines the session runs as written). Each joint event has a clear division of roles.
Read each body's own description on the institute's clubs and committees pages (this was done on 1 November 2026; some pages carry old dates, so confirm every line before writing).
A short note via the faculty advisor, stating one session, the exact role of the body and what the club brings. Nothing is agreed until the body replies.

Role map: Quizzar runs scoring and the microphone for the guessing game (Session 4); Datonics suggests a dataset and reads what pairs produce (Sessions 7 and 10); Finserve checks the EMI calculator before it is shown (Session 18); Markaizen gives feedback on the campaign and the Media Cell approves anything before it is posted (Session 21); the T and D Cell vets CVs and mock interviews (Career Lab); the E&I Cell provides mentors or judges for the Sell It track and for startup-style events (Neural Fest); the Industrial Relations and Sponsorship Committee owns corporate relations, so any company approach for Neural Fest goes to it first; The Dialectical Society structures cases, moderates and trains moderators for AI on Trial (Session 16); the Media and Communications Committee co-runs the AI-powered campaign event.
Approvals: the faculty advisor approves each request and is copied on every message.
Faculty advisor's sign-off; one-page session note per body.
Campus Liaison (owner); Faculty Advisor; Curation Lead.
Better-run sessions, shared audiences and credibility inside the institute.
Credit the body in the recap; invite its members to Build Day and Demo Day; ask what it wants from the club.
Number of co-delivered sessions held; satisfaction of the partner body; share of sessions that ran as written when a body declined.
Run joint activities with peer clubs and neighbouring institutes, starting with online, low-cost formats.

LEAP AI Club at Plaksha; GDG Chandigarh; the IIT Mandi iHub; DSG and E-Cell at IIT Roorkee; 100xEngineers; IIM Shillong's business-technology club; other IIMs and nearby colleges including one with no club like this.

Peers say yes faster than companies. A fellow IIM is a lighter collaboration than a company. Cross-campus venture pairing, with technical builders and go-to-market and finance leads in mixed teams, is one route; including a college with no AI club is another.

Pick peer clubs whose own page invites collaboration and publishes a club contact (for example LEAP and GDG chapters). Approach clubs directly first and use an institutional contact only as a fallback.

A two-hour virtual cross-campus build session with mixed teams choosing a business problem, building a lightweight demo and presenting it; both clubs shape the brief, recruit participants and document the best outputs. Or a 60-minute online beginners session with one volunteer mentor followed by a joint mini challenge. Or a joint design challenge (IIT Mandi iHub).
Month 1 to 2: send the peer-club letter to two or three clubs.
Month 3 to 4: hold the first joint session; document outputs.
Month 6: open Session 12 to two outside teams online.
Month 11: invite outside teams to Think It and Sell It at Neural Fest (V1-11).
Video link, joint brief, shared recap, judges from both sides.
Campus Liaison for inter-IIM clubs; Partnerships Manager; Projects Lead.
Wider reach, new mentors and a stronger Neural Fest field.
Share the recap and each side's credit; propose the next joint event only after the first works.
Joint sessions held; outside teams at Session 12 and Neural Fest; repeat collaboration.
Obtain platform access, tool credits, event hosting and, where sensible, prizes, in exchange for real value to the partner.

Student platforms (Unstop and similar), AI companies with campus programmes (Sarvam AI, Krutrim, Fetch.ai Innovation Lab), financial-literacy and interview-preparation platforms (StockGro, InterviewBuddy), and the institute's edtech partner (Futurense).

The clearest routes are published programmes: Unstop's host-with-Unstop route and Igniters Club programme, Sarvam's Campus and Champions programmes, StockGro's campus partnership page, Krutrim's past cloud credit offers.
Prefer partners with a published campus programme or a record of sponsoring student events (track records exist for Krutrim, Fetch.ai Innovation Lab, InterviewBuddy, StockGro and Unstop).

Pitch product adoption and real usage, not banner space: participants use the partner's platform on real business problems and send structured feedback. Offer in return a named thank-you on the page and at the event, a short post-event report with photographs and anonymous feedback, and an honest user perspective. Make one specific, small ask, such as two mentors, tool credits or a prize. Never promise attendee data or exclusivity. Pilot first: a one-event concept with a clear owner and output. Apply for community programmes such as Sarvam Champions only after the club has run two events and has evidence of community execution.
Prepare the one-page event note and an itemised budget.
Send to the publisher's official route.
Offer a tiered recognition menu: partner tier on event material, short demo or workshop slot, participant access, report.
After approval, confirm in writing: deliverables, branding use and approvals, timelines.
Deliver, then close the loop (V2-15).
Event note, budget, partner logo-use approval, registration page, report template.
Sponsorship Lead (owner); Partnerships Manager; Faculty Advisor; Industrial Relations and Sponsorship Committee where required.
Platform listing for Neural Fest, tool credits for Build Day participants, prizes and mentors.
Quarterly update; invitation to judge; renewal conversation after the second event.
Partners approached; in-kind or cash support secured; partner renewals; conversion from pilot to recurring.

initiatives.title: Professional Bodies and Academic Speaker Network

items.t: Build a roster of faculty and professional-body speakers who can give short, narrow talks across the year, instead of relying on one willing professor.

The ICAI AI Committee faculty pool and the Bombay Chartered Accountants' Society Technology Initiatives Committee; IIT, IISc and other academics proposed for the curriculum; named individual speakers.

A committee with a trained pool of faculty gives the club a roster across the year rather than one evening, and finance and commerce bodies fit the annual-report, money, ethics and back-office sessions. Five academics have work that matches themes in the curriculum.

Read what the speaker actually works on and propose something narrow drawn from it: for a finance body, how a finance professional uses these tools in a working day; for a decision-making researcher, why we trust a confident answer; for the academics on the list, generative models, enterprise AI, human-AI collaboration, technology adoption and AI digital agents.

Write to the person, never the institution. Open with one checked reference to their work and name the topic. Offer a 30-minute online talk, ten minutes of questions, a feedback note, and a fallback of a ten-minute recorded reply. Where the proposer has a personal connection to a body, say so in the first line (this is required; neither body has a relationship with the club today). Use the faculty advisor on institute letterhead where the route is institutional.
Month 0: faculty advisor approves the first two bodies and three academics.
Month 1: send the expert-session letter; ask for one faculty member from a pool, not an institutional tie-up.
Month 2 to 3: schedule one session aligned to Sessions 9, 14 or 18.
Re-check office-bearers and committee pages before writing (office bearers change every year).
Expert-session template, video link, question form, faculty advisor letter.
Academic Liaison (owner); Faculty Advisor; Speaker Liaison.
A roster of expert speakers and credibility with professional bodies.
Thank-you and student-feedback note; invite to Demo Day; offer to co-host a webinar once a track record exists.
Talks delivered; speakers per body; repeat engagements; faculty feedback.
Win editorial reach, not advertising, through a small number of media relationships that value student explainers.
Analytics India Magazine; the institute's own Media Cell; podcasts and other outlets cited by speakers.
Paid media costs are out of reach, so the club asks for editorial and community support. An editor can judge a finished piece but not a promise.
Choose outlets that already write about Indian AI daily and have a published community or partnership route.

Media template: propose student-written pieces on how students actually use tools for study, money and internships; offer a student-written Demo Day recap or an interview with a club member; no payment; the editor decides what is published; ask for a pointer to one practitioner who enjoys talking to beginners. Write one eight-hundred-word piece first so the email is an offer, not a request.
Month 3 to 5: write the first recap or explainer, approved by the Media Cell.
Month 5: send the media letter with two paragraphs of concept and three sample headlines.
Month 9 to 12: pitch the Neural Fest story.
Respect the one follow-up rule.
One finished piece, sample headlines, Media Cell approval.
Media Lead; Social and Content Lead; Faculty Advisor.
One or two published pieces; a speaker referral; Neural Fest coverage.
Send follow-up recaps and offer exclusives only when real; credit the outlet.
Pieces published; referrals; reach of published pieces.
Turn every session into reusable, consent-cleared content that builds the club's identity and demonstrates its work to partners.
Students, prospective members and partners who check the club's presence before replying to a pitch.

A monthly session can create value beyond its hour; branding work is listed (colour, type, tone, an AI myths-busted carousel, a profile grid of nine posts that read together); and partners are more likely to respond to a club with a visible track record. The branding files referred to were not available when this plan was prepared.

Not stakeholder-specific; the audience is defined by channel: Instagram for students (reels, carousels), LinkedIn for partners and alumni (recaps, projects), a club page or Field Guide public section for resources.

Content types: short screen recordings of a tool or concept; reels and short clips (before-and-after prompt comparisons, quick explanations, challenge highlights); carousel posts (key takeaways, common mistakes, definitions, step-by-step explainers); a session recap with useful prompts, links and resources. Fixed series: weekly Did-you-know; AI Radar monthly; AI myths busted; family safety card; AI Wrapped awards post. Tone: no jargon, no hype, no promising what a tool cannot do.

Rules: only pre-approved demonstrations and outputs are captured; no private participant conversations, personal data or identifiable outputs without permission; use demo accounts and fictional examples; the featured member must agree before anything is made about them.
Before each session: tick which activities may be recorded.
During: capture only approved items.
Within 24 hours: post the session recap (prompts, links, resources).
Within the week: edit approved clips into one carousel and one reel.
Anything under the institute's name goes to the Media Cell first.

Pick a visual identity once the branding materials are reviewed (colour pairs with published contrast, three fonts, one icon set, an eight-point grid are the specifics offered in the branding contents index).
Free design tools, a consent form, a content calendar, a Media Cell contact.
Social and Content Lead (owner); Content and Field Guide Editor; Media Lead.
A coherent, consent-clean public presence and a library of proof for partner pitches.
Tag and credit partners and guests (with approval); send partners the recap link.
Recap posted within 24 hours for every session; content engagement and reach; share of public content with consent on file.
Use the club's learning to protect and educate the wider campus and nearby communities.
All IIM Sirmaur students; families (through the safety card); nearby colleges with no AI club.

A family safety card on deepfakes and UPI scams is a deliverable of Session 15, and a myths-busted carousel is a piece of content. A Mythbusters event, a Deepfake Detective event and a Fact-versus-Fiction page are also options. These are naturally public.
Campus groups through the Media Cell; nearby colleges via faculty advisor; student communities.

Short, visual, forwardable items: the family safety card, a myths-busted carousel, a verify-it checklist, a labelling debate summary. Invite one nearby college with no such club to a session ([Added in synthesis]: a shared online session).
After Session 15: publish the safety card.
After Session 5: publish the three-step check.
Once a term, an open campus session on a public-interest topic (deepfakes, scams, data rights).
Invite the nearby college to one open session.
Design tools; Media Cell approval; consent.
Awareness Lead; Social and Content Lead.
A public-interest profile and goodwill beyond the club.
Credit contributors; follow up with the invited college.
Campaign pieces published; shares and forwards; outside attendees at open sessions.

initiatives.title: Neural Fest and Demo Day Outreach

items.t: Fill Neural Fest and Demo Day with outside teams, judges, problem setters, platforms and media, without over-promising.
IIT Mandi, NIT Hamirpur, the Chandigarh colleges, the other IIMs and one nearby college with no club; industry judges and problem setters; a platform for registration; a media partner.
Neural Fest is the only item in the plan that could outgrow the club, and it needs approval, a room and a date. Industry judges sit on Demo Day. Platform and sponsor routes are proposed.
Use V2-01 and V2-08. Route every company through the Industrial Relations and Sponsorship Committee first.

Industry comes in as judges and problem setters, not banner sponsors, in year one; a company that writes a problem statement has a reason to send people. Offer outside teams an online route for Think It and Sell It against the same rubric with no travel funding. Ask platforms to list the event and host registration. Pitch prize-pool or credit support only with a defined benefit (an example ask to Kreyato AI is platform access for all competing teams and a prize contribution; an ask of that scale, with a promise of 200 or more competing teams, is unrealistic for a first event and should be scaled to the club's record; [Added in synthesis]).
T minus 12 weeks: approval, room, date; open the partner list.
T minus 8: invitations to outside clubs; problem-setter asks; platform listing.
T minus 4: registration opens; two mentoring evenings.
T minus 2: judges confirmed; media pitch.
T minus 0: event.
T plus 5 days: thank-yous, results, recap and report to partners (V2-15).
Event note, rubric, registration page, judge brief, partner pack.
Event Outreach Lead; Projects Lead; Faculty Advisor; IRS Committee.
Outside participation across tracks, at least three judges and one problem setter, a media piece.
Invite judges and problem setters to the next Demo Day; give outside clubs an invitation to co-host next year.
Outside registrations; judges and problem setters confirmed; platform listing secured; media pieces; partner satisfaction.
Turn one-off interactions into lasting relationships by always closing the loop and showing partners what their contribution achieved.
Every partner, speaker, mentor and sponsor who has engaged.

Closing the loop within five days is a core stage; sponsors are promised a named thank-you and a short report; and a log records what each company offered. A reputation for follow-through makes later asks easier.
Everyone logged in the pipeline ledger who has given time, content or money.

Within five days: thanks, attendance against RSVP, an anonymous feedback summary, approved photos or links, outcomes and one specific next-step proposal. For sponsors: a short report with photographs, participation numbers, projects built and honest product feedback. Publish no partner logo without written approval.
Template the report; fill it within five days.
Log what each partner offered and what they received.
Measure partner value: approved content reach, voluntary product trials, useful product feedback and willingness to repeat.
Hold an annual partner review in Month 11; retire inactive relationships.
Hand the ledger to the next team in the handover pack.
Report template, ledger, photos with consent.
Partnerships Manager; Pipeline Keeper; Social and Content Lead.
Higher repeat rate; partners who refer the club onward.
Quarterly short update; invitation to Demo Day; recognition on the club page with approval.
Reports sent within five days (target 100%); repeat and referral rate; partner-reported satisfaction.
